source.title: Concept-Guided Interpretability via Neural Chunking
source.authors: Shu-Chen Wu; S. Alaniz; Shyamgopal Karthik; Peter Dayan; Eric Schulz; Zeynep Akata

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary information are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that focusing on individual neurons is insufficient and presents population-level chunks as interpretable alternatives. Its own experiments concern chunks, not neuron-pole job counts or the specific explanation and attribution-graph tests in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses neuron polysemanticity and the limits of neuron-level interpretability, but those background claims are supported by citations. Its own relevant results measure population chunks and interventions on them; they do not audit positive or negative neuron poles, score neuron explanations on new activating text, or test attribution graphs.
record.test_reason: The paper's own experiments extract population-level chunks from residual-stream activity (LLaMA-3-8B, T5, RWKV, Mamba, small RNNs) and graft or freeze them. It never audits individual MLP neuron poles, InceptionV1 neurons, attribution graphs or simulation-scored neuron explanations. Its statements that neurons are polysemantic and that monosemantic neurons are a small fraction come only from citations in Related Work, not from its own results. That makes it discussion, not a T5 argument backed by results.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors propose the Reflection Hypothesis, that population activity mirrors data regularities, and conclude that chunking extracts interpretable population-level entities: words, POS tags and narrative schemas. Grafting these chunks causally alters model behaviour.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses population averaging, unsupervised chunk discovery, and discrete sequence chunking to identify population-level patterns; it does not use the pole-based neuron audit or neuron-explanation scoring methods described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that grafting effectiveness varies by target word and intervention layer; early-layer grafting is most effective in the tested layer groupings. It also notes that population averaging may be less effective for context-sensitive words such as prepositions.

fits_no_version.finding: SI E.1: in LLaMA-3 residual streams, PA finds concept encoding supported by substantial populations of dimensions; the authors say sparse encodings of concepts are rare.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLaMA-3-8B residual streams, word concepts are decodable mainly from distributed subpopulations rather than single dimensions.

fits_no_version.finding: Population-averaging chunks predicted selected concepts better than the most active SAE latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested concepts, population chunks out-decode individual SAE latents in LLaMA-3-8B.

fits_no_version.finding: Grafting population chunks raises target-word occurrence in generations (Tables 1, 3, 5, 6). The effect is strongest for concrete words and early layers, and weak for prepositions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Population-level concept chunks causally steer generation, with effectiveness depending on word type and layer.

record.problems: The paper does not directly test neuron-pole interpretability or any of the listed neuron-explanation claims. Its relevant population-chunk results use selected models and concepts; the reported grafting effects vary substantially by target concept and layer. Some word-detection performance is described qualitatively in the text rather than with numerical scores.
record.rows_left_out: Other chunk-detection and intervention results are not cataloged because they concern the paper's broader chunking method rather than the listed claim versions; examples include the TREC category and layer results in Table 1, freezing results in Table 4, narrative-schema decoding, and RNN experiments.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job-share estimates.
No neuron-pole job shares across models, MoE or scale.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron analysis.
No test of architecture, regularization or tools versus interpretable-neuron share.
No neuron-based attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
No test of whether activating-example explanations predict neuron firing.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T5 is downgraded to T6: the anti-neuron statements are cited background, not the paper's own results. The analysed units are residual-stream dimensions, not MLP neurons or poles, so even the SI E.1 remark about distributed encoding does not bear on V1 or V2.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or estimates of neuron poles' one-job, two-job, or unexplained shares.
No comparison of pole-job shares across model scales, dense and MoE architectures, or models up to trillions of parameters.
No study of InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
No test of vision-model interpretability estimates or whether architecture, regularization, and tools explain them.
The paper grafts population chunks and measures changes in generation, but does not build attribution graphs or test their explanatory sufficiency or reconstruction error.
No test of whether explanations written from activating examples predict where individual neurons fire.
No automated scoring of individual-neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared population-averaging chunks with individual concept-related SAE neurons as decoders on test data.

conditions.value: selected example words including cheese, cake, and cheesecake

rows.measure: Prediction of concept occurrence from neural activity
rows.baseline: Individual concept-related neurons identified by a pretrained SAE
rows.value: Population-averaging chunks predicted the selected concepts better than the individual SAE neurons; the paper describes high true positives and low false positives across layers.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison, not numerical scores. This compares population chunks with selected SAE neurons, not pole-job explanations.
rows.check: The baseline is pretrained SAE latents (EleutherAI sparsify), not the model's own neurons, and the comparison is qualitative only. It is the study's method compared with another method, so it bears on no version.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3-8B

rows.uncertainty: Figure 5 error bars denote standard error of the mean.
rows.note: The text does not state numerical detection rates. This measures population chunks, not neuron poles.

tranche.reason: The paper tests population chunks in residual-stream activity, not neuron poles, neuron explanations or attribution graphs.
